title: Stuck on a number sequence? Look at the gaps
description: Try differences, multipliers and alternating patterns before reaching for a complicated rule.

sections.title: Look between the numbers
sections.html:
Consider 4, 7, 10, 13. Instead of staring at the values, ask what happens from one to the next. Each step adds three, so 16 is a natural continuation.

Write the differences underneath: +3, +3, +3. You have turned four numbers into a simpler pattern. The same move can reveal a rule that was difficult to see in the original line.

sections.title: What if the gaps are changing?
sections.html:
Try 2, 5, 10, 17. The gaps are +3, +5, +7. Continuing with the next odd gap, +9, gives 26. Check your rule against every displayed step, not just the last two numbers.

Now compare 3, 6, 12, 24. The gaps are growing, but repeated doubling gives a much simpler explanation. Differences are a first tool, not the only one.

sections.title: Sometimes there are two interleaved lines
sections.html:
For 2, 10, 4, 20, 6, 30, separate alternate positions. The first, third and fifth terms are 2, 4, 6; the second, fourth and sixth are 10, 20, 30. A plausible next term is 8.

On paper, use two colours or two rows. That is more reliable than trying to keep both patterns floating in your head. When a sequence swings between small and large values, this is worth a quick check.

Continue 5, 9, 15, 23 using gaps that increase by two.

33. The gaps are 4, 6 and 8; the next is 10, so 23 + 10 = 33.

sections.title: A plausible pattern is not a mathematical proof
sections.html:
A finite list can fit many rules. Without a stated rule, ‘the next number’ is not always uniquely determined. Puzzle questions generally intend a simple pattern supported by all the clues and answer choices.

Use a short checklist: constant difference, repeated multiplier, changing differences, alternating lines. Then read the available answers. If your rule needs a fresh exception at every step, try a simpler explanation before committing.

When you get one wrong, record the type of pattern you missed. ‘I forgot to test alternate terms’ is a more useful note than ‘I am bad at sequences’.

sources.name: University of Cambridge NRICH — Patterns, sequences and structure

practice: Open Sequence and try the checklist on a round. Use the explanation to check whether your rule fits all the terms.
